step_explanations.title: Validate Training Data
step_explanations.description: Ensure labeled documents exist for at least 2 classes.
step_explanations.why_it_matters: SVM is a supervised classifier requiring labeled training data.

step_explanations.title: Vectorize Documents
step_explanations.description: Convert text to TF-IDF vectors, creating a numerical feature matrix.
step_explanations.why_it_matters: SVM operates on numerical vectors, not raw text.

step_explanations.title: Find Maximum-Margin Hyperplane
step_explanations.description: Optimize the SVM objective to find the weight vector w and bias b that maximize the margin.
step_explanations.why_it_matters: The hyperplane defined by w and b is the actual classifier - it determines all future predictions.

step_explanations.title: Predict New Document
step_explanations.description: Compute decision value f(x) = w·x + b and predict class based on sign.
step_explanations.why_it_matters: This is the actual classification step used on new, unseen documents.

formula_cards.title: SVM Decision Function
formula_cards.explanation: The SVM predicts class based on the sign of the decision function, where w is the weight vector and b is the bias.

formula_cards.title: Maximum Margin Objective
formula_cards.explanation: SVM minimizes weight magnitude (for large margin) plus a penalty for misclassified examples.
formula_cards.example: C=1.0 balances margin width and classification errors

formula_cards.title: Kernel Trick
formula_cards.explanation: Kernels implicitly map features to higher-dimensional space where classes are separable.
formula_cards.example: RBF kernel: K(x,y) = exp(-γ||x-y||²) maps to infinite-dimensional space

hover_annotations.definition: Regularization parameter - controls trade-off between margin width and classification errors.
hover_annotations.formula_meaning: Larger C = less regularization = fewer training errors but potentially overfitting
hover_annotations.example: C=1.0 is default; C=100 means almost no regularization
hover_annotations.common_mistake: Thinking larger C always improves performance (it can cause overfitting)

hover_annotations.definition: Training samples that lie on or within the margin boundary - they define the decision boundary.
hover_annotations.formula_meaning: Only support vectors affect the decision function f(x) = Σ αᵢyᵢK(xᵢ,x) + b
hover_annotations.example: 3 support vectors means only 3 training samples matter for predictions
hover_annotations.common_mistake: Thinking all training samples are support vectors (most have αᵢ=0)

references.title: Support-Vector Networks
references.relevance: Original SVM paper introducing the soft margin and kernel trick.

references.title: A Tutorial on Support Vector Machines for Pattern Recognition
references.relevance: Comprehensive tutorial on SVM theory, kernels, and applications to text classification.

references.title: Text Classification using SVMs: Fast Training, Practical Application
references.relevance: Shows linear SVMs with TF-IDF features are highly effective for text classification.

receiver_mode_explanations.explanation: SVM draws a line between positive and negative reviews, keeping it as far from both groups as possible.
receiver_mode_explanations.teaching_notes: Visualize with 2D features first. Show how the margin works.

receiver_mode_explanations.explanation: SVM solves min ½||w||² + C×Σξᵢ to find the maximum-margin hyperplane. Prediction: f(x) = w·x + b.
receiver_mode_explanations.technical_detail: Linear kernel is standard for text (high-dim sparse features). RBF kernel can model non-linear boundaries but is rarely needed for text.

receiver_mode_explanations.explanation: Linear SVMs are state-of-the-art for high-dimensional sparse text features. Research shows they often match or beat deep learning on small-to-medium text datasets (Wang & Manning, 2012).
receiver_mode_explanations.technical_detail: Limitations: no probability output by default (use Platt scaling), sensitive to feature scaling. For text, scaling is less critical since TF-IDF is already normalized.

receiver_mode_explanations.explanation: LinearSVC in sklearn is O(n_samples × n_features) per iteration. Use hinge loss with SGD for large datasets. C=1.0 is a reasonable default.
receiver_mode_explanations.technical_detail: Complexity: train O(n×d×iterations), predict O(d). Memory: O(d) for weight vector. API: sklearn.svm.LinearSVC or sklearn.svm.SVC(kernel='linear').

receiver_mode_explanations.explanation: SVM introduces the concept of margins and support vectors. Great for teaching optimization in ML.
receiver_mode_explanations.teaching_notes: Quiz: What's the effect of C? Exercise: Plot decision boundary with 2D features. Show support vectors vs. other points.

research_context: SVMs were introduced by Cortes & Vapnik (1995) and became the dominant ML algorithm in the 1990s-2000s. For text classification, linear SVMs with TF-IDF features consistently rank among the best methods, even in the deep learning era.

teaching_notes.summary: SVM finds the maximum-margin hyperplane to separate text classes in feature space.
quiz_questions: What does the C parameter control in SVM?
Why are linear kernels preferred over RBF for text classification?
What are support vectors and why do they matter?
classroom_demo_tips: Visualize the margin with 2D features (reduce TF-IDF to 2D with PCA for demo)
Show how C affects the decision boundary
Compare number of support vectors with training set size
common_misconceptions: SVM always needs a kernel trick (false - linear SVM is most common for text)
More support vectors = better model (false - fewer is often better, indicating wider margin)
